MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Rheumatoid Arthritis:
Definition & The Core Concept

Rheumatoid arthritis = a chronic autoimmune inflammatory disease causing chronic synovitis → a symmetrical, deforming polyarthritis of the small joints, with systemic + extra-articular features.

The core concept — an autoimmune synovitis: the immune system attacks the synovial lining → it becomes inflamed, thickened and proliferates into a destructive “pannus” that erodes cartilage and bone. This explains everything: the inflammatory pain pattern (worse with rest, better with use, prolonged morning stiffness — the opposite of osteoarthritis), the symmetrical small-joint distribution sparing the DIPs, the deformities, the systemic features, and the treatment (immunosuppression with DMARDs).
Priorities: early diagnosis + early DMARDs (a “window of opportunity” before irreversible damage), and recognising extra-articular complications (esp. atlantoaxial subluxation). Classic patient: a woman (pre-menopausal women affected 3× more), HLA-DR4, smoker.

Pathophysiology — The Pannus
🔥
Autoimmune chronic synovitisThe inflamed synovial lining (of joints, tendon sheaths, bursae) thickens and is infiltrated by inflammatory cells.
↓

Risk factors: female (pre-menopausal 3×), family history, HLA-DR4, smoking (→ citrullination → anti-CCP).
The Antibodies
🧬 Rheumatoid factor (RF)
  • Present in ~70%
  • An autoantibody — usually IgM against the Fc portion of the patient's own IgG
  • → immune activation + systemic inflammation
🎯 Anti-CCP (ACPA)
  • More sensitive AND specific than rheumatoid factor
  • Often PRE-DATES the disease (predicts who will develop it)
  • Linked to smoking (citrullination)
The rule: anti-CCP is more specific + sensitive than rheumatoid factor and can pre-date disease; rheumatoid factor is IgM against the Fc of IgG. “Seronegative” disease (clinically rheumatoid but negative serology) occurs in ~20–30%.
Clinical Features & Hand Deformities

The 3 joint symptoms: pain, stiffness, swelling — worse with rest, improves with activity; early morning stiffness >30 min. Symmetrical distal polyarthritis of the small joints — most commonly MCP, PIP, wrist, MTP; the DIP is not affected.

🔎 On examination
  • Tenderness + synovial thickening → a “boggy” feeling
  • Systemic: fatigue, weight loss, flu-like illness, muscle aches + weakness
🔁 Palindromic rheumatism
  • Self-limiting episodes of inflammatory arthritis lasting a few days then fully resolving (normal joints between)
  • Rheumatoid factor / anti-CCP positivity → may progress to established rheumatoid arthritis

Atlantoaxial Subluxation — An Emergency
In the cervical spine, synovitis + damage to the ligaments around the odontoid peg of the axis (C2) allows it to shift within the atlas (C1). Subluxation can cause spinal cord compression = an emergency.
High-yield: must be considered before a general anaesthetic requiring intubation (neck manipulation risks cord compression) → MRI as part of the pre-operative assessment.

High-yield syndromes: Felty's (rheumatoid + splenomegaly + low WCC), Caplan's (rheumatoid + pneumoconiosis nodules), rheumatoid nodules. Rheumatoid arthritis also ↑ cardiovascular disease risk (accelerated atherosclerosis) — a leading cause of death.
Investigations
NICE: urgent rheumatology referral for persistent synovitis (within 3 weeks); consider NSAID + baseline bloods while waiting. Initial assessment: rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP, CRP, ESR; X-ray hands/feet; USS or MRI to detect synovitis when unclear.

Management
Principle: early DMARDs (treat-to-target) + bridging steroids; escalate to combination/biologics; the goal is remission before irreversible joint damage.
💊

↓
🧬

↓
🎯
Treat-to-target + MDTAim for remission/low disease activity (monitored by DAS28), escalating until achieved. Physiotherapy, OT, analgesia/NSAIDs (+PPI), cardiovascular risk, surgery for damaged joints. Methotrexate monitoring: FBC/LFTs (myelosuppression/hepatotoxicity; teratogenic).
Vaccinations: annual influenza + 5-yearly pneumococcal (immunosuppressed); avoid live vaccines.

MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Osteoarthritis:
Definition & The Core Concept

Osteoarthritis (OA) = “wear and tear” of the synovial joints — degeneration of articular cartilage, especially in weight-bearing joints and the CMC, DIP and PIP joints of the hands.

The core concept: a degenerative, mechanical (non-inflammatory) joint disease — cartilage breaks down faster than it can repair. This drives everything: a mechanical pattern (pain worse with activity / end of day, minimal morning stiffness — the opposite of inflammatory arthritis), structural X-ray changes (the LOSS mnemonic), and largely non-pharmacological / symptomatic management (no immune process to suppress).
The commonest arthritis; strongly linked to age, obesity and joint loading. The key distinction is OA (mechanical/degenerative) vs rheumatoid arthritis (inflammatory/autoimmune).

Morning stiffnesstransient (<30 min)prolonged (>30–60 min)
Hand jointsDIP (Heberden's) + PIP (Bouchard's) + CMC (squaring)MCP + PIP + wrist (spares DIP)

The rule: OA = mechanical pain, brief stiffness, DIP involvement, no systemic features; rheumatoid = inflammatory pain, prolonged stiffness, MCP/wrist, systemic. OA affects the DIP joints (Heberden's); rheumatoid spares them — a key hand discriminator.
Risk Factors & Pathogenesis
⚖️ Risk factors
  • Increasing age
  • Obesity
  • Occupation (farmers, labourers — joint loading)
  • Female sex; family history
🔬 Pathogenesis
  • Abnormal stress + loading → mechanical cartilage damage
  • Imbalance: cartilage damage > chondrocyte (repair) response
  • → progressive cartilage loss → bone-on-bone → osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis + cysts, joint-space narrowing
Clinical Features

Joint pain (the main symptom) + stiffness: worse with activity + at the end of the day (mechanical); morning stiffness only transient (<30 min) — a key discriminator from rheumatoid.

🦴 General signs
  • Bony enlargement of the joint
  • Restricted range of movement
  • Crepitus (grating) on movement
  • Effusions around the joint (sometimes)
✋ Hand signs
  • Heberden's nodes — DIP joints
  • Bouchard's nodes — PIP joints
  • Squaring at the thumb base — CMC joint
Hand mnemonic: Heberden's = Higher (DIP, further out); Bouchard's = Bottom/Below (PIP). Commonly affected: knees, hips, hands (DIP/PIP/CMC), lumbar + cervical spine, first MTP.

Investigations
NICE — a clinical diagnosis WITHOUT investigations if: patient over 45, typical activity-related pain, and no morning stiffness (or <30 min). Investigate only if atypical or to exclude another diagnosis.

LLoss of joint space
OOsteophytes (bony spurs)
SSubchondral Sclerosis

X-ray findings correlate POORLY with symptoms (severe changes can be asymptomatic + vice versa) → treat the patient, not the X-ray.

Bloods are normal (normal inflammatory markers; no autoantibodies).
Management
Principle: non-pharmacological core FIRST → topical then oral NSAIDs → joint replacement for severe hip/knee; avoid strong opioids.
🏃
Non-pharmacological — the core (first-line)Education, weight loss, occupational therapy, and EXERCISE (muscle strengthening + aerobic) for everyone — a core treatment (improves pain + function).
↓
💊

↓
🦿
SurgicalHip → total hip replacement; knee → total knee replacement — for severe symptoms/function despite conservative treatment.
Current (NICE 2022): exercise + weight management as the core, topical NSAIDs first, and against paracetamol as routine monotherapy and against strong opioids.
Exam Pearls
What it is
Degenerative “wear and tear” of synovial joints; weight-bearing joints + hands (DIP/PIP/CMC); risk factors = age, obesity, occupation, female, family history.
Mechanical pattern
Pain WORSE with activity/end of day, brief (<30 min) morning stiffness.
Hand signs
Heberden's (DIP) + Bouchard's (PIP) + squaring of the thumb base (CMC); bony enlargement, crepitus, restricted ROM.
Diagnosis
CLINICAL if >45 + activity-related pain + no/brief morning stiffness; bloods normal.
X-ray = LOSS
Loss of joint space, Osteophytes, Subchondral sclerosis, Subchondral cysts (poorly correlate with symptoms).
Management
Core = education + exercise + weight loss; topical → oral NSAIDs (+PPI); intra-articular steroids; joint replacement (hip/knee) for severe; avoid strong opioids.
MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Lyme Disease:
Definition & The Core Concept

Lyme disease (Lyme borreliosis) = a tick-borne infection caused by the spirochaete Borrelia burgdorferi, transmitted by Ixodes (hard) ticks.

The core concept: a multisystem infection that evolves in stages — a localised skin lesion (erythema migrans) at the bite, then, if untreated, disseminating to neurological, cardiac and joint disease weeks–months later. Key point: erythema migrans is a CLINICAL diagnosis — treat immediately, don't wait for serology (often negative early).
A great mimic — facial palsy (mimics Bell's), heart block, arthritis. Acquired from tick bites in wooded/grassy areas; doxycycline first-line.
Which Stage?
StageTimingFeatures
Early localiseddays–weekserythema migrans (the rash) ± flu-like symptoms
Early disseminatedweeks–monthsneuroborreliosis (facial palsy, meningitis, radiculopathy), carditis (heart block), multiple erythema migrans
Latemonths–yearsLyme arthritis (large joints), chronic neurological, acrodermatitis chronica atrophicans
Erythema Migrans — The Hallmark
🎯 Erythema migrans
  • A red lesion that increases in size, may have central clearing (“bull's-eye”/target)
  • Usually 1–4 weeks after a bite (range 3 days–3 months); lasts several weeks
  • Typically ≥5 cm, NOT itchy or painful
↔️ vs tick-bite reaction
  • A hypersensitivity reaction appears within 48h and is itchy
  • Erythema migrans is later, expanding, and not itchy
The rule: erythema migrans = diagnose Lyme clinically + treat immediately; do NOT wait for blood tests (serology is often negative this early).
Disseminated & Late — The Great Mimic
SystemFeature
Neurological (neuroborreliosis)facial nerve (CN VII) palsy — can be bilateral (mimics Bell's); meningitis; painful radiculopathy
Cardiac (Lyme carditis)heart block (atrioventricular — can fluctuate / be complete); myo/pericarditis → cardiology
Rheumatological (Lyme arthritis)acute/subacute mono- or oligoarthritis of LARGE joints (esp. knee), relapsing — a late feature
Skin (late)acrodermatitis chronica atrophicans (late skin atrophy); borrelial lymphocytoma (early)
High-yield: Lyme is a key cause of bilateral facial nerve palsy → test for it in facial palsy (esp. with tick exposure or bilateral involvement). Lyme carditis → heart block (can be complete but often reversible with treatment).
Investigations
🎯
Erythema migrans presentCLINICAL diagnosis, no testing needed → treat immediately.
↓
🧪
No rash but suspected → ELISA (IgM + IgG)If negative but symptoms persist → repeat ELISA in 4–6 weeks (antibodies take time — early serology can be falsely negative).
↓
🔬
ELISA positive → immunoblot (Western blot)Confirms the diagnosis. Neuroborreliosis: serum antibody (± CSF). Don't exclude Lyme on a single negative test if suspicion is high.
Management (NICE NG95)
Principle: prompt antibiotics — doxycycline first-line; regimen depends on the manifestation; treat erythema migrans immediately without waiting for tests.
💊 Antibiotics
  • Doxycycline 100 mg BD × 21 days (erythema migrans / early)
  • Amoxicillin 1 g TDS × 21 days if doxycycline contraindicated (pregnancy, young children)
  • Neuroborreliosis → higher-dose doxycycline or IV ceftriaxone
  • Carditis / severe → IV ceftriaxone + cardiac monitoring; arthritis → oral (longer course)
Watch for
  • Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction — fever/chills shortly after starting (spirochaete death; not an allergy)
  • Children <18 → specialist unless a single erythema migrans with no other symptoms
  • Prevention: tick avoidance + prompt removal
Exam Pearls
What it is
Tick-borne (Ixodes) infection with Borrelia burgdorferi (spirochaete); staged, multisystem.
Stages
Early = erythema migrans; disseminated = facial palsy / heart block / meningitis; late = arthritis (large joints).
Erythema migrans
Expanding “bull's-eye” rash ≥5 cm, 1–4 weeks post-bite → CLINICAL diagnosis → treat immediately (don't wait for serology).
The great mimic
Bilateral facial (CN VII) palsy (vs Bell's), heart block (Lyme carditis), large-joint arthritis (knee).
Investigations (no rash)
ELISA first → immunoblot to confirm; repeat ELISA in 4–6 weeks if early + negative; don't exclude on one negative test.
Management
Doxycycline 100 mg BD × 21 days (1st-line); amoxicillin if pregnant; IV ceftriaxone for CNS/cardiac; warn about Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction.
MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Juvenile Idiopathic:
Definition & The Core Concept

Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) = persistent joint inflammation (arthritis) lasting ≥6 weeks, presenting before age 16, with no other identified cause — the commonest chronic inflammatory joint disease of childhood.

The core concept: JIA is an umbrella term for several distinct subtypes — they share childhood-onset chronic arthritis but differ in pattern, associated features and complications. The key task is recognising which subtype (management + complications differ). Two threads run through all: screening for uveitis (a silent, sight-threatening eye complication) and, for the systemic subtype, watching for macrophage activation syndrome.
A diagnosis of exclusion. Subtypes are defined by the first ~6 months; ANA + uveitis risk, and rheumatoid factor status, help stratify.
The Decisive Fork — Which Subtype?
SubtypePatternKey features
Oligoarticular≤4 joints — commonestyoung girls, large joints (knee), ANA positive → high UVEITIS risk, best prognosis
Polyarticular≥5 jointssymmetrical, small + large joints; rheumatoid-factor-negative (younger) or -positive (like adult rheumatoid — worse)
Systemic (Still's)arthritis + systemic featuresfever, salmon rash, etc. (see below)
Enthesitis-relatedarthritis + enthesitisolder boys, HLA-B27, juvenile spondyloarthropathy (sacroiliitis, acute anterior uveitis)
Psoriaticarthritis + psoriasispsoriasis, dactylitis, nail pitting
High-yield subtypes: oligoarticular (commonest, uveitis risk); systemic/Still's (fever + rash); polyarticular (rheumatoid-factor-positive = adult-rheumatoid-like); enthesitis-related (HLA-B27, older boys).
Systemic-Onset JIA (Still's Disease)
🌡️ The classic picture
  • High spiking (quotidian) fever — daily spikes
  • Salmon-pink evanescent rash — appears with the fever
  • Lymphadenopathy, arthritis, uveitis
  • Anorexia + weight loss / malaise
🔬 Also
  • Hepatosplenomegaly, serositis (pericarditis/pleuritis), myalgia
  • Raised ferritin, rheumatoid factor + ANA NEGATIVE, neutrophilic leucocytosis
Key complication — macrophage activation syndrome (MAS): a life-threatening haemophagocytic syndrome (cytopenias + very high ferritin + organ dysfunction). Systemic JIA = the childhood equivalent of adult-onset Still's disease.
Clinical Features (General)
🦵 Arthritis
  • Joint pain, swelling, warmth, stiffness (esp. morning + after inactivity — inflammatory)
  • Limp / refusal to weight-bear, reduced function
  • In young children: limp, irritability, milestone regression, or avoiding a joint rather than complaining of pain
👁️ Uveitis
  • Chronic anterior uveitis — often asymptomatic (“silent”) but sight-threatening
  • → regular slit-lamp screening (esp. ANA-positive oligoarticular JIA)
Systemic features (fever, rash, lymphadenopathy) point to the systemic subtype; chronic disease + steroids can cause growth impairment.
Investigations
JIA is a CLINICAL diagnosis of exclusion — arthritis ≥6 weeks, onset <16, no other cause. Exclude septic arthritis, reactive arthritis, malignancy (leukaemia), trauma, other connective tissue disease.
🩸
FBC
Anaemia, ↑WCC/platelets; cytopenias → think leukaemia or MAS.
🔥
ESR / CRP / ferritin
Raised (esp. systemic); ferritin very high in systemic/MAS.
🧬
ANA / rheumatoid factor / HLA-B27
ANA + → uveitis risk (oligoarticular); rheumatoid factor + polyarticular = worse; HLA-B27 → enthesitis-related.
👁️
Slit-lamp exam
Screen for silent, sight-threatening uveitis, even if asymptomatic.
Exclude malignancy: a child with bone pain, cytopenias, or systemic features → exclude leukaemia before attributing to JIA. Imaging: ultrasound/MRI (synovitis, effusions), X-ray (later damage).
Management
Principle: MDT care — control inflammation, screen for + treat uveitis, and preserve growth + function.
💊
NSAIDs → corticosteroidsNSAIDs for symptom relief. Intra-articular steroid injections (especially effective in oligoarticular JIA); systemic steroids for systemic/severe disease (steroid-sparing strategy — growth concerns).
↓
🧬

↓
👁️

Arthritis ≥6 weeks, onset <16, no other cause; commonest chronic childhood arthritis; diagnosis of exclusion.
Subtypes
Oligoarticular (≤4 joints — commonest, ANA+, UVEITIS risk, best prognosis); polyarticular (≥5 joints; RF+ = adult-rheumatoid-like, worse); systemic/Still's (fever + rash); enthesitis-related (older boys, HLA-B27); psoriatic.

NSAIDs → intra-articular/systemic steroids → methotrexate → biologics (anti-TNF; IL-1/IL-6 for systemic); uveitis screening; MDT + monitor growth.
MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__GALS (Gait, Arms, Le:
Definition & The Core Concept

GALS = Gait, Arms, Legs, Spine — a rapid musculoskeletal screening examination used to detect significant MSK abnormalities in a symptomatic or at-risk patient.

The core concept: GALS is a quick screen, not a full joint exam — its purpose is to rapidly identify whether a MSK problem exists and roughly where, so you can then do a detailed regional exam (look–feel–move) of the abnormal area. Built on screening questions + observing a few key movements; takes ~2 minutes; a core OSCE station.
Used as the first step; any abnormality → focused regional REMS (Regional Examination of the Musculoskeletal System).
The Three Screening Questions
❓
“Any pain or stiffness in your muscles, joints or back?”Screens PAIN / STIFFNESS.
↓
👕
“Can you dress yourself completely without any difficulty?”Screens fine function — upper limb + hands.
↓
🪜
“Can you walk up and down stairs without any difficulty?”Screens gross function — lower limb + gait.
The logic (high-yield): these three screen pain and both fine + gross motor function — “no” to all three makes significant MSK disease unlikely; a “yes” directs your attention.
The Examination — General Principles
🧭 Setup
  • Introduction / consent / exposure (underwear ± shorts)
  • Compare both sides, look for symmetry
  • Order: Gait → Arms → Legs → Spine (with standing inspection near the start)
🔁 The recurring principle
  • Inspect (look) → assess movement (move)
  • A full regional exam adds feel (palpate for warmth/tenderness/swelling)
  • GALS is mainly look + move
G — Gait
🚶 What to do
  • Ask the patient to walk a few metres, turn, and walk back
  • Observe smoothness + symmetry, stride length, arm swing
  • The phases (heel strike + toe-off) and turning
Abnormal gaits
  • Antalgic (painful — shortened stance on the painful side)
  • Trendelenburg (hip abductor weakness)
  • Shuffling/festinant (Parkinsonian), broad-based/ataxic (cerebellar), foot drop
The point: gait integrates the whole lower limb + spine + neurological function — a quick, sensitive screen.
Inspection (Standing)

With the patient standing, inspect from front, side and behind:

ViewLook for
From behindshoulder + gluteal bulk/symmetry, scoliosis, level iliac crests, popliteal swelling (Baker's cyst), hindfoot (valgus)
From the sidenormal spinal curvatures — cervical lordosis, thoracic kyphosis, lumbar lordosis (↑kyphosis / loss of lumbar lordosis → ankylosing spondylitis)
From the frontshoulder/limb symmetry, muscle bulk, joint swelling/deformity, quadriceps bulk, knee (varus/valgus), forefoot
A — Arms
💪 What to do
  • “Put your hands behind your head” — shoulder abduction + external rotation
  • Inspect the hands (palms up then down): swelling, deformity, muscle wasting
  • “Make a fist” + “touch each fingertip to your thumb” — power grip + precision
🤏 Key sign
  • Squeeze across the MCP joints — tenderness suggests inflammatory (e.g. rheumatoid) joint disease
  • Assess wrist/elbow, pronation/supination
The point: screens the shoulder girdle + hand function (the “can you dress yourself?” question examined).
L — Legs

With the patient lying on the couch:

🦵 What to do
  • Inspect for swelling, deformity, quadriceps wasting
  • Hip: passive internal rotation (flex hip + knee to 90°, rotate) — often the first movement lost in hip pathology
  • Knee: flexion + extension, feel for crepitus; patellar tap / bulge test for an effusion
🦶 Feet
  • Inspect; squeeze across the MTP joints (tenderness = inflammatory)
  • Check for callus/deformity
The point: hip internal rotation + knee effusion are the highest-yield lower-limb screens.
S — Spine
🧍 What to do
  • Cervical: “tilt your ear to your shoulder” (lateral flexion); also flexion/extension/rotation
  • Lumbar: “bend forward and touch your toes” — fingers on the lumbar spine feel the vertebrae separate on flexion
  • Inspect for scoliosis/kyphosis; temporomandibular joint (“open your mouth”) sometimes included
🎯 High-yield link
  • Reduced vertebral separation on lumbar flexion → ankylosing spondylitis (links to Schober's test)
The point: lumbar flexion (toe-touch) + cervical lateral flexion are the core spine screens.
Recording GALS

Recorded as a grid documenting Appearance (A) and Movement (M) for each domain — a tick (✓) if normal or a cross (✗) with a note if abnormal:

DomainAppearanceMovement
Gait✓ / ✗ (overall)—
Arms✓ / ✗✓ / ✗
Legs✓ / ✗✓ / ✗
Spine✓ / ✗✓ / ✗
The point: a normal screen is quickly documented as all ticks; any cross flags the area for detailed REMS examination.
Exam Pearls
What it is
GALS = Gait, Arms, Legs, Spine — a rapid MSK screen (not a full joint exam) to detect + localise pathology → then do focused REMS.
Three screening questions
(1) pain/stiffness in muscles/joints/back? (2) dress yourself without difficulty? (3) walk up/down stairs? — screen pain + fine + gross function.
Gait

MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Fibromyalgia:
Definition & The Core Concept

Fibromyalgia = a chronic pain syndrome of widespread musculoskeletal pain, fatigue, sleep disturbance and cognitive dysfunction, in the absence of an identifiable inflammatory or structural cause.

The core concept: a disorder of central pain processing (central sensitisation, abnormal neurotransmitter signalling) — not a disease of the joints or muscles. Hence all investigations are normal and it is a clinical diagnosis of exclusion. Manage it primarily non-pharmacologically — the evidence base has shifted decisively toward exercise first.
Common (>2% of adults); more common in women; strongly associated with mood disorders, poor sleep and other functional syndromes (IBS, chronic headache). Overlaps heavily with chronic fatigue syndrome.

MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Compartment Syndrome:
Definition & The Core Concept

Compartment syndrome = raised pressure within a closed anatomical (fascial) compartment → compromised tissue perfusion → ischaemia and necrosis — a surgical emergency.

The core concept: muscles are bound within non-expandable fascial compartments. Rising pressure (bleeding/swelling) eventually exceeds capillary/venous perfusion pressure → blood can't get in → muscle + nerve become ischaemic → necrosis — all while the arterial pulse may still be present. So the diagnosis is clinical and urgent — waiting for pulselessness is waiting too long.
The whole message: pain out of proportion to the injury (especially on passive stretch) → suspect compartment syndrome → urgent fasciotomy. Most commonly follows fractures — classically supracondylar (elbow) and tibial shaft.

The rule: pain beyond what's expected, especially on passive stretching, and a patient using excessive/max-dose analgesia → suspect compartment syndrome — the earliest + most reliable signs.

Keep limb LEVEL, remove tight casts, urgent FASCIOTOMY (± amputation); aggressive IV fluids for rhabdomyolysis/AKI. Complication: Volkmann's contracture.
MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bursitis:
Definition & The Core Concept

Bursitis = inflammation of a bursa — a small fluid-filled sac that cushions and reduces friction between bone and overlying soft tissue.

The core concept: a bursa reduces friction, so bursitis is an overuse / pressure / friction (or infection) problem at a specific, superficial site — a localised, well-circumscribed swelling over a bony prominence. Two priorities: (1) identify which bursa (location gives the diagnosis), and (2) decide whether it's infected (septic) — which changes management from conservative to antibiotics/drainage.
Common; usually self-limiting; the key don't miss is septic bursitis.

The rule: hot, red, exquisitely tender bursa ± fever ± a skin breach → septic bursitis → aspirate + antibiotics. If in doubt, aspirate + send for microscopy/culture (± crystals). Superficial bursae (olecranon, prepatellar) are most prone to septic bursitis.

Not a true cyst but a distension of the gastrocnemius–semimembranosus bursa behind the knee. Primary = no underlying pathology, usually children; secondary = an underlying condition (e.g. osteoarthritis), usually adults.
The DVT mimic: a ruptured cyst → symptoms like a DVT (calf pain, redness, swelling) → must be distinguished from a true DVT (most ruptures are asymptomatic). Management: none needed in children; treat the underlying cause in adults.

💊 Septic bursitis

  • Antibiotics covering Staph aureus (flucloxacillin)
  • Incision + drainage if severe / not resolving

MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone Tumours:
Definition & The Core Concept

Bone tumours = neoplasms arising in bone — benign or malignant, and primary (from bone) or secondary (metastases).

The core concept — organise by three questions: benign or malignant? primary or secondary? and (for primaries) what age + cell of origin? Radiographic appearance + patient age + location together give a reliable diagnosis. The single most important point: metastases (secondary) are far commoner than primary bone tumours → in an adult with a bone lesion, think mets first.
Red flags for malignancy: persistent bone pain (esp. night pain), a mass, and unexplained pathological fracture — must not be dismissed. Among primaries the X-ray signs are pathognomonic (Codman/sunburst, onion-skin, soap-bubble).
The Decisive Fork — Benign vs Malignant, Primary vs Secondary
Primary vs secondary: secondary (metastatic) tumours are the COMMONEST bone malignancy overall. The classic primaries (mnemonic “lead kettle” / PB-KTL): Prostate, Breast, Kidney, Thyroid, Lung → in an adult, a bone lesion is a metastasis until proven otherwise. Multiple myeloma = the commonest primary bone malignancy in adults (a plasma-cell tumour) → lytic “punched-out” lesions.

  • Chondrosarcoma: surgical resection (chemo/radio-resistant — surgery is key)

MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Adult-Onset Still's:
Definition & The Core Concept

Adult-onset Still's disease (AOSD) = a rare systemic autoinflammatory disorder — the triad of high spiking fever, arthralgia/arthritis and an evanescent salmon-pink rash.

The core concept: the adult form of systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis — autoinflammatory (innate immune, cytokine-driven) rather than autoantibody-driven. This explains its two lab fingerprints: seronegative (rheumatoid factor and ANA negative) but with a markedly raised ferritin. Fundamentally a diagnosis of exclusion using the Yamaguchi criteria.
Rare; bimodal age (15–25 and 35–45); can be self-limiting, relapsing or chronic.

CategoryMust exclude
Infectionsepsis, endocarditis, viral (EBV, CMV, parvovirus, HIV, hepatitis), TB
Malignancylymphoma (can mimic exactly), leukaemia, solid tumours

The rule: AOSD is a diagnosis of exclusion — the seronegativity (rheumatoid factor / ANA negative) + very high ferritin point toward it, but infection, lymphoma and other autoimmune disease must be excluded first.

FeatureDetail

High-yield: the fever spikes daily in the late afternoon/evening and the salmon-pink rash appears with the fever spike and fades between — this time-locked fever-rash coupling is highly characteristic. Also: sore throat (a very common early symptom), hepatosplenomegaly, serositis.
Investigations

There is no single diagnostic test — it's a clinical diagnosis of exclusion.

🔺
Ferritin
Markedly raised (often >1000) — the acute-phase marker of choice for monitoring; low glycosylated fraction adds specificity.
🧬

🔥

Raised inflammatory markers; neutrophilic leucocytosis; anaemia of chronic disease.
🧪

Often deranged.
Yamaguchi criteria: major — fever ≥39°C ≥1 week, arthralgia ≥2 weeks, typical rash, leucocytosis; minor — sore throat, lymphadenopathy/splenomegaly, abnormal LFTs, rheumatoid factor + ANA negative; plus exclusion of infection/malignancy/other rheumatic disease.
Complications
Macrophage activation syndrome (MAS) — the key life-threatening complication: a form of haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) — uncontrolled immune activation → very high fever, cytopenias, very high ferritin, hepatosplenomegaly, deranged LFTs/coagulation → a medical emergency. Suspect if a Still's patient deteriorates with falling cell counts + rising ferritin.
Also: serositis (pericarditis, pleuritis), chronic destructive arthritis, hepatitis.

Principle: NSAIDs → corticosteroids → DMARDs/biologics (especially IL-1 and IL-6 blockade).

Systemic autoinflammatory disorder; triad = high spiking fever + arthralgia + salmon-pink rash; bimodal age (15–25, 35–45).

Quotidian (daily) spike, late afternoon/evening, with the evanescent salmon-pink rash; often sore throat.

A diagnosis of exclusion (rule out infection, lymphoma, SLE / rheumatoid arthritis) using the Yamaguchi criteria.
Key complication
Macrophage activation syndrome (MAS/HLH) — deteriorating patient with cytopenias + soaring ferritin → emergency.
Management
NSAIDs (≥1 week trial) → corticosteroids → methotrexate / IL-1 (anakinra) / IL-6 (tocilizumab) / anti-TNF.

Definition & The Core Concept

Chronic fatigue syndrome / myalgic encephalomyelitis (ME/CFS) = a chronic, disabling multisystem condition whose central feature is persistent, debilitating fatigue made worse by activity, not explained by another condition.

The core concept: ME/CFS is a clinical diagnosis of exclusion built around one defining, high-yield feature — post-exertional malaise (PEM) — and the modern management has been fundamentally rewritten (NICE 2021): the old “push through with graded exercise” approach is now rejected as potentially harmful, replaced by energy management / pacing that respects the patient's limits.
Cause unclear; often follows a viral infection (including COVID → overlaps with “long COVID”); commoner in women; can be profoundly disabling.

The rule: ME/CFS = disabling fatigue + post-exertional malaise + unrefreshing sleep + cognitive dysfunction, lasting ≥3 months, with other causes excluded. Post-exertional malaise is the discriminating feature — its presence is now required for the diagnosis (NICE 2021).

  • Disproportionate to the level of exertion
  • Often delayed (hours to up to ~72 hours later)
  • Prolonged, with abnormally slow recovery
  • Accompanied by loss of strength / function
Why it matters
  • Because exertion worsens the illness, PEM is the reason graded/incremental exercise is NOT appropriate and can cause harm
  • This is the crux of the modern management change

Overview — crystal arthropathies
Arthritis caused by crystal deposition within joints, provoking an acute inflammatory (hot, red, swollen) monoarthritis. The two to know are gout (monosodium urate) and pseudogout (calcium pyrophosphate, CPPD).
The organising principle: identify the crystal on polarised light microscopy of joint aspirate. Gout = needle-shaped, negatively birefringent urate; pseudogout = rhomboid, positively birefringent CPPD.

What & why
Gout = a crystal arthropathy caused by deposition of monosodium urate crystals in joints, associated with chronically high blood uric acid (hyperuricaemia).
The core concept: too much urate → crystals precipitate in the joint → intense inflammation. Three defining features: the acute presentation (a sudden, exquisitely painful, hot, swollen joint — classically the big toe), the diagnostic crystals (needle-shaped, negatively birefringent monosodium urate), and a two-part management — treat the acute flare separately from long-term urate-lowering. The key acute point: you cannot clinically distinguish gout from septic arthritis → always aspirate.
  • Common; classically a middle-aged man; strongly linked to diet, alcohol, diuretics, and renal function.

The rule (high-yield): an acute hot swollen joint MUST have septic arthritis excluded by joint aspiration (if suspected → emergency aspiration + antibiotics); crystals present does NOT exclude co-existing infection. Pathogenesis
  • Hyperuricaemia from overproduction of uric acid OR renal underexcretion — urate crystals deposit → inflammation; over time → gouty tophi.
  • Risk factors: male, family history, obesity, high-purine diet (meat, seafood), alcohol, thiazide diuretics, cardiovascular disease, CKD, chemotherapy (↑cell turnover), TB drugs (pyrazinamide, ethambutol), haemolytic anaemia.
High-yield: the two classic drug causes are thiazide diuretics and pyrazinamide. Purines → uric acid: high-purine foods (red meat, seafood, offal) + alcohol (esp. beer) + high cell turnover (chemo, haemolysis) → ↑urate.
Gouty tophi
Gouty tophi = subcutaneous uric acid deposits, typically on the hands, elbows, and ears — a sign of chronic tophaceous gout (long-standing/undertreated); their presence is an indication for urate-lowering therapy (§7).

Overview — seronegative spondyloarthropathies
A family of inflammatory arthritides that are rheumatoid-factor negative (“seronegative”), HLA-B27 associated, and share axial involvement, enthesitis and extra-articular features.
The organising principle: think HLA-B27 + enthesitis (inflammation where tendon/ligament meets bone) + asymmetrical large-joint/axial disease + shared extra-articular features (anterior uveitis, IBD, psoriasis, dactylitis). Contrast with rheumatoid arthritis (symmetrical small joints, RF/anti-CCP positive).

What & why
Ankylosing spondylitis = a chronic inflammatory condition of the axial skeleton (mainly the spine + sacroiliac joints), causing progressive stiffness and pain, that can progress to fusion (ankylosis) of the spine and sacroiliac joints.
The core concept: the prototype seronegative spondyloarthropathy — an HLA-B27-associated, RF-negative inflammatory arthritis targeting the axis (spine + SI joints) and the entheses (where tendons/ligaments insert into bone), not the small peripheral joints of rheumatoid. Signature: inflammatory back pain in a young man (worse with rest, better with movement, night/morning waking, prolonged stiffness). Its tendency to fuse the spine produces the classic late deformity, plus a cluster of extra-articular associations (the 7 A's). Priorities: recognise inflammatory back pain, confirm sacroiliitis, and use exercise + NSAIDs + anti-TNF.

The principle: exclude/treat septic arthritis first; treat the triggering infection; NSAIDs ± steroids; usually self-limiting.
  • Treat the trigger — e.g. chlamydia (+ partner treatment for STI). NSAIDs first-line for joint symptoms.

Clinical image placeholder: SLE malar (butterfly) rash — erythema across the cheeks and nasal bridge sparing the nasolabial folds
Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) = a chronic, multisystem autoimmune disease driven by autoantibodies against nuclear components — causing inflammation in skin, joints, kidneys, blood, serosa, and CNS.
The core concept: the archetypal antinuclear-antibody, immune-complex (type III hypersensitivity) disease — antibodies against self nuclear material (DNA, histones) form immune complexes that deposit in tissues → inflammation everywhere. Hence it is multisystem and relapsing-remitting. Anchors: the autoantibody profile, complement + anti-dsDNA tracking activity, and hydroxychloroquine as the backbone. Two "don't miss": lupus nephritis and antiphospholipid syndrome.
  • Classic patient: a young/middle-aged woman, more common in Asian, African, Caribbean, and Hispanic people.
Pathophysiology
  • Apoptotic cells are cleared inefficiently → self-antigens (nuclear constituents) are presented to T cells → B cells make autoantibodies against the nuclear antigens.
  • The antibodies form immune complexes → deposit in tissues → activate complement → chronic inflammation (a type III hypersensitivity reaction).
  • Associations: HLA-B8, DR2/DR3; relapsing-remitting course.
The core defect: defective clearance of apoptotic material → exposure of nuclear antigens → antinuclear autoantibodies → immune complexes → multisystem inflammation.
Clinical features (multisystem)

Non-specific: fatigue, malaise, mouth ulcers, lymphadenopathy, fever, weight loss.

The rule: ANA to screen (sensitive), anti-dsDNA + anti-Smith to confirm (specific); anti-dsDNA also tracks activity.
  • FBC: anaemia of chronic disease, leucopenia, thrombocytopenia (cytopenias common).
  • Inflammatory markers: use ESR (CRP may be normal in active disease) — a raised CRP should prompt a search for infection.
  • Complement (C3 + C4) DECREASED in active disease (consumed) → low complement + high anti-dsDNA = active disease.
  • Lupus nephritis: high urine protein:creatinine ratio; renal biopsy to confirm + classify.
  • Also anti-Ro/anti-La (Sjögren's overlap; neonatal lupus/heart block risk) and antiphospholipid antibodies (§6).
Monitoring disease activity
Activity markers: ↑ anti-dsDNA = more active; ↓ complement (C3/C4) = more active; ↑ ESR (CRP usually normal — if raised, think infection). The rule: rising anti-dsDNA + falling complement = a flare.
Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) — associated condition

SLE is strongly associated with antiphospholipid syndrome — antiphospholipid antibodies (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, anti-β2-glycoprotein) → a prothrombotic state:

  • CLOTs: Coagulation (arterial + venous thrombosis), Livedo reticularis, Obstetric (recurrent miscarriage), Thrombocytopenia.
The paradox (high-yield): despite a prolonged APTT in vitro, patients are hypercoagulable in vivo. Management: aspirin (prophylaxis) / anticoagulation (warfarin) after thrombosis; LMWH + aspirin in pregnancy. (See the Antiphospholipid Syndrome tab.)
Management
The principle: sun protection + hydroxychloroquine backbone; escalate to steroids/immunosuppressants/biologics by severity + organ involvement.
  • General: photosensitive rash → sunscreen + sun avoidance; NSAIDs for arthralgia/serositis.
  • 1st line: hydroxychloroquine — the backbone (reduces flares, improves skin/joint disease + survival; monitor for retinopathy).
  • Corticosteroids — for flares/active disease and internal organ involvement.
  • Severe/organ disease: DMARDs — methotrexate, mycophenolate mofetil, cyclophosphamide (mycophenolate/cyclophosphamide for lupus nephritis); biologics — rituximab (anti-CD20) and belimumab (targets B-cell activating factor, BAFF).
  • Lupus nephritis: immunosuppression + BP/proteinuria control (ACE inhibitor) — the key organ to protect. Manage cardiovascular risk, APS, and pregnancy (anti-Ro → neonatal lupus/heart block; continue hydroxychloroquine).
Drug-induced lupus (in brief)
A milder, usually reversible lupus from drugs — hydralazine, isoniazid, procainamide — with anti-HISTONE antibodies (anti-dsDNA negative); arthralgia/serositis/rash but renal + CNS involvement rare; resolves on stopping the drug. See the Discoid & Drug-Induced Lupus tab for detail.

Two distinct "lupus" entities to distinguish from systemic lupus (SLE): Discoid lupus erythematosus (DLE) = a chronic, scarring, skin-ONLY autoimmune condition; Drug-induced lupus (DIL) = a milder, usually reversible SLE-like syndrome triggered by specific drugs.
The core concept: the lupus family spans a spectrum — DLE (skin only) → SLE (multisystem) → DIL (drug-triggered, milder, reversible). For DLE: recognise the scarring, photosensitive, disc-shaped lesions (+ small risk of SLE/SCC). For DIL: recognise the culprit drugs + anti-histone antibodies and that it resolves on drug withdrawal.

  • A chronic autoimmune skin condition, presenting at 20–50 years; more common in women, darker skin, and smokers.
Two key risks: <5% progress to SLE (most stay skin-limited → monitor for systemic features); rarely long-standing scarred lesions transform to squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) → biopsy any changing lesion.

  • Photosensitive lesions, typically on the face, scalp, and ears (sun-exposed areas).

  • A lupus-like syndrome where not all typical SLE features are seen, and which usually resolves on stopping the drug.
  • Features: arthralgia + myalgia (commonest); skin (malar rash) + pulmonary involvement (serositis) common; renal + CNS involvement RARE.
The rule: DIL = arthralgia/myalgia + rash/serositis, but SPARES the kidneys and CNS → milder, reversible.

MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Vasculitis:
Overview — vasculitis
📷
Diagram placeholder: vasculitis classified by vessel size — large (GCA, Takayasu), medium (PAN, Kawasaki) and small (ANCA-associated: GPA/MPA/EGPA; and IgA vasculitis) — with palpable purpura as the classic small-vessel skin sign
Inflammation of blood vessel walls leading to ischaemia and organ damage. Vasculitides are classified by the size of vessel predominantly affected (large / medium / small).
The organising principle: vessel size predicts the presentation. Large-vessel (GCA, Takayasu) → cranial/limb ischaemia; small-vessel ANCA-associated (GPA, EGPA, MPA) → a pulmonary–renal picture. PMR is closely linked to GCA.

What & why
📷

Giant cell arteritis (GCA), or temporal arteritis = a systemic vasculitis of medium + large arteries — a granulomatous inflammation, classically of the cranial branches of the aorta (esp. the temporal artery).
The core concept: a MEDICAL EMERGENCY because it threatens irreversible vision loss — inflamed arteries occlude → optic nerve ischaemia → sudden, permanent blindness, and once one eye is affected the other is at risk within days. So: suspect it, and treat with high-dose steroids IMMEDIATELY — don't wait for the biopsy. Strong link with polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR); classic patient >60 with new headache + scalp tenderness + jaw claudication.
  • The commonest primary systemic vasculitis in adults over 50; affects the elderly (rare <50).

The rule: no visual/jaw symptoms → oral prednisolone 40–60 mg; visual/jaw claudication/ischaemia → IV methylprednisolone — both started ASAP, before biopsy. Jaw claudication (jaw pain on chewing — masticatory ischaemia) is a red flag for imminent visual loss.
Clinical features

Typical: >60 with a (usually unilateral) headache.

FeatureDetail

Vision loss = anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy (AION): occlusion of the posterior ciliary artery → optic nerve ischaemia; fundoscopy = swollen, pale optic disc with blurred margins; typically sudden + painless + irreversible. Associated PMR features: shoulder + pelvic girdle pain/stiffness, systemic symptoms, muscle tenderness.
The PMR link
  • GCA has a strong link with polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR) — ~40–50% of GCA patients have PMR features; ~15% of PMR patients develop GCA.
  • PMR = bilateral shoulder + pelvic girdle pain/stiffness (worse in the morning), elderly, raised ESR + dramatic steroid response.
The rule: ask about girdle pain/stiffness in GCA (PMR), and about headache/visual/jaw symptoms in PMR (GCA) — always screen for the other.
Investigations
  • 1st line: ESR — markedly raised (often >50, frequently >100); CRP also raised.
  • Temporal artery biopsy (gold standard): multinucleated giant cells (granulomatous inflammation); may be NORMAL due to SKIP LESIONS (patchy → a negative biopsy doesn't exclude GCA → take a long segment >1 cm); do it within ~1–2 weeks of starting steroids.
  • Duplex ultrasound: the "halo sign" (hypoechoic halo) + stenosis — increasingly first-line (non-invasive).
Critical rule: do NOT delay treatment for investigations — start steroids on clinical suspicion; the biopsy/ESR confirm afterwards.
Management
The principle: high-dose steroids IMMEDIATELY (before biopsy) — IV if visual/ischaemic, oral if not — + aspirin, PPI, bone protection; slow taper over 1–2 years; tocilizumab for relapsing/refractory.
  • Steroids ASAP: no visual symptoms → prednisolone 40–60 mg; visual/jaw symptoms → IV methylprednisolone 500 mg–1 g (×3 days) then high-dose oral; once confirmed → slow wean over 1–2 years (guided by symptoms + ESR/CRP); start before biopsy.
  • Adjuncts: aspirin 75 mg (↓vision loss + stroke), PPI (gastroprotection), bone protection — bisphosphonate + calcium + vitamin D while on steroids.
  • Tocilizumab (anti-IL-6): for relapsing/refractory GCA or to reduce steroid exposure (methotrexate is an alternative steroid-sparing agent). Urgent ophthalmology for any visual symptoms.
Prognosis: untreated → ~15–20% get permanent visual loss (AION); once one eye is affected, the fellow eye is at high risk within days → hence immediate steroids.
Exam pearls
What it is
Granulomatous medium/large-vessel vasculitis of the elderly (>50); MEDICAL EMERGENCY — irreversible vision loss.
Classic
>60 + new (unilateral) headache + scalp tenderness (brushing hair) + jaw claudication + tender/thickened, pulseless temporal artery.
Vision loss
Anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy (AION) — posterior ciliary artery occlusion → swollen pale disc; sudden, painless, irreversible; fellow eye at risk within days.
PMR link
Strong link with PMR (girdle pain/stiffness) — always screen for the other.
Investigations
↑↑ESR (+CRP); temporal artery biopsy (giant cells; SKIP LESIONS → can be normal); duplex "halo sign" — but DON'T delay treatment.
Management
Steroids IMMEDIATELY — no visual symptoms → oral prednisolone 40–60 mg; visual/jaw → IV methylprednisolone; taper over 1–2 years; + aspirin + PPI + bone protection; tocilizumab for relapsing/refractory.
What & why
Polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR) = an inflammatory condition causing pain + stiffness in the shoulders, pelvic girdle, and neck.
The core concept: a disease of inflammatory girdle STIFFNESS in the elderly — the key word is stiffness, not weakness (power is normal). Two distinctive things: a rapid, dramatic, near-diagnostic response to low-dose steroids, and a strong link to giant cell arteritis (GCA) (screening for GCA is mandatory). Largely a clinical diagnosis of exclusion — bloods are non-specific (raised ESR with a NORMAL CK, ruling out a true myopathy). Classic: over 60 with new bilateral shoulder + hip girdle pain and prolonged morning stiffness.
  • Strong association with GCA (~15% of PMR develop GCA) → always ask about GCA symptoms.
The decisive fork: PMR vs its mimics (a diagnosis of exclusion)

The rule: PMR = clinical features + steroid response + excluding differentials (SLE, rheumatoid, myeloma, myositis, hyperparathyroidism, lung cancer). Crucial discriminator from myositis = the NORMAL CK. PMR causes stiffness, NOT true weakness — power is normal on resisted movements.
Clinical features

Rapid onset (<1 month) of bilateral early-morning stiffness, in over-60s; must be present ≥2 weeks for diagnosis.

High-yield: pain/stiffness worse in the morning + after rest, interferes with sleep, takes ≥45 min to ease — prolonged morning stiffness (≥45 min) in the shoulder + pelvic girdles = the PMR hallmark. Also systemic symptoms (weight loss, fatigue, fever), muscle tenderness, carpal tunnel. Always screen for GCA (headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, visual symptoms).
Investigations
  • Diagnosis is CLINICAL — characteristic features + response to steroids + excluding differentials.
  • Inflammatory markers: ESR raised (CRP too) — but non-specific.
  • CK + EMG NORMAL — excludes a myopathy/myositis (the key discriminating test).
  • Exclude differentials: FBC, U&E, LFT, TFT, calcium, protein electrophoresis (myeloma), CK, RF/anti-CCP, ± CXR.
The steroid-response test: a dramatic response to low-dose steroids (near-complete resolution within days) supports the diagnosis; failure to respond → reconsider (look for a mimic). The rule: >60 + bilateral girdle pain/stiffness ≥45 min + raised ESR + NORMAL CK + dramatic steroid response = PMR.
Management
The principle: low-dose oral prednisolone (dramatic response) + a slow reducing regimen over 1–2 years, with steroid safety measures + bone protection.
  • NICE regimen: prednisolone 15 mg daily → follow up after 1 week (expect a dramatic response); typically 1–2 years with a reducing regime: 15 mg until controlled → 12.5 mg for 3 weeks → 10 mg for 6–10 weeks → then reduce by 1 mg every 4–8 weeks.

Bone protection: alendronate + calcium/vitamin D immediately. Steroid-sparing / relapsing: methotrexate (or tocilizumab). Monitor symptoms + ESR/CRP at each reduction; watch for GCA developing at any point.

Inflammatory bilateral pain + STIFFNESS of the shoulders + pelvic girdle + neck in the over-60s; NO true weakness (normal power).

Rapid onset (<1 month), bilateral, morning stiffness ≥45 min, worse after rest, ≥2 weeks duration.

Strong link (~15% get GCA) → always screen for GCA (headache, jaw claudication, visual symptoms).

CLINICAL diagnosis — raised ESR but NORMAL CK + EMG (excludes myositis); dramatic steroid response; exclude rheumatoid, SLE, myeloma, myositis, hyperparathyroidism, lung cancer.

PMR = stiffness + normal CK; myositis = weakness + ↑↑↑CK.

Prednisolone 15 mg daily (dramatic response), slow taper over 1–2 years; "DON'T STOP" — don't stop abruptly (adrenal crisis), sick-day rules, treatment card, osteoporosis prevention (+PPI); bone protection.
What & why
📷
Clinical image placeholder: GPA — “saddle-nose” deformity from nasal septal/cartilage destruction; and CT/CXR cavitating pulmonary nodules
Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA), formerly Wegener's = a necrotising, granulomatous vasculitis of small-to-medium vessels — one of the ANCA-associated vasculitides (AAV), classically affecting the upper + lower respiratory tract + kidneys.
The core concept: the "ENT + lung + kidney" ANCA vasculitis — a pulmonary-renal syndrome with prominent upper-airway (ENT) involvement. Two recognisable features: granulomatous, destructive ENT disease (epistaxis, sinusitis, saddle-nose deformity) and its serology cANCA (anti-PR3). Untreated it's rapidly fatal (necrotising glomerulonephritis + pulmonary haemorrhage) → recognise the triad, test cANCA, start aggressive immunosuppression.
  • Any age (peak middle age); a medical emergency when it threatens the kidneys/lungs.

Also scleritis/proptosis (orbital granuloma), purpura, mononeuritis multiplex, arthralgia, constitutional symptoms.
Investigations
  • ANCA: cANCA (anti-PR3) — highly specific (positive in ~90% of systemic disease); also check pANCA/anti-MPO.
  • Urinalysis + renal function: haematuria, proteinuria, red cell casts, rising creatinine (screen the kidneys).
  • Imaging: CXR/CT chest — nodules, cavities, infiltrates, pulmonary haemorrhage; sinus imaging.
  • Biopsy (definitive): renal (necrotising, crescentic, pauci-immune glomerulonephritis) or lung/ENT (granulomatous necrotising vasculitis). Raised CRP/ESR, anaemia.

The principle: aggressive immunosuppression in two phases — INDUCTION (steroids + rituximab or cyclophosphamide) then MAINTENANCE (rituximab/azathioprine); an emergency in organ-threatening disease.

  • Adjuncts: PJP (pneumocystis) prophylaxis (co-trimoxazole — also reduces relapse), bone protection, monitor toxicity + infection.
Prognosis: GPA relapses in ~50% within 5 years (esp. PR3-ANCA positive) → long-term monitoring (symptoms, ANCA, renal function). Untreated GPA is rapidly fatal (necrotising glomerulonephritis + pulmonary haemorrhage) → treat early + aggressively.

Necrotising GRANULOMATOUS small-to-medium vessel vasculitis; an ANCA-associated vasculitis.

MPA (pANCA/anti-MPO, no granulomas); Churg-Strauss/EGPA (pANCA + asthma + eosinophilia).

cANCA, urinalysis (haematuria/casts) + renal function, CT chest (nodules/cavities), biopsy (necrotising granulomatous / pauci-immune crescentic glomerulonephritis).

Induction — steroids + RITUXIMAB (preferred) or cyclophosphamide (>80% remission); maintenance — rituximab/azathioprine; PJP prophylaxis; relapses ~50%; untreated = fatal.
What & why
📷
Clinical image placeholder: Behçet's — oral and genital aphthous ulcers, and a positive pathergy test
Behçet's disease = a complex, chronic, multisystem inflammatory disorder of the blood vessels and tissues — a variable-vessel vasculitis that can involve the eyes, skin, GI tract, vessels, MSK, and CNS.
The core concept: a disease of recurrent inflammation + ulceration, its defining near-universal feature being recurrent oral (aphthous) ulcers — with genital ulcers, eye disease, and skin lesions completing the picture. A clinical diagnosis (no single test), relapsing-remitting. Distinctiveness: the "Silk Road" distribution (Turkey, Iran, Japan), the HLA-B51 association, and the pathergy reaction (skin hypersensitivity to a needle prick). Be alert to sight-threatening (uveitis) and life-threatening (vascular/neuro/GI) complications.

Recurrent painful ORAL ulcers (sharply circumscribed, red halo, ~3×/year, heal in 2–4 weeks) + GENITAL ulcers.

Eyes (uveitis, retinal vasculitis — sight-threatening), skin (erythema nodosum, acne-like), GI (ileocaecal ulcers — mimics IBD), MSK (arthritis), vascular (arterial aneurysms + venous DVT/Budd-Chiari), CNS (neuro-Behçet's).

Unusual — prothrombotic.

CLINICAL (recurrent oral ulcers + ≥2 other features); pathergy test (needle prick → erythema/induration at 24–48h; also positive in Sweet's, pyoderma gangrenosum).

Topical steroids (mouth) + topical anaesthetic (genital) + colchicine + systemic steroids for flares; immunosuppression (azathioprine) + biologics (infliximab/anti-TNF) for severe organ disease.
MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Metabolic Bone Disea:
Overview — metabolic bone disease
Disorders of bone quantity, quality or turnover — distinct from inflammatory or structural bone disease. The three to know are osteoporosis, osteomalacia and Paget's disease.
The organising principle: read the bone profile (Ca, PO₄, ALP, PTH, vitamin D). Osteoporosis = low bone mass with normal biochemistry; osteomalacia = defective mineralisation; Paget's = disordered remodelling (isolated ↑ALP).
DiseaseCa / PO₄ / ALPHallmark & treatment

An isolated raised ALP with normal Ca/PO₄ in an older patient → think Paget's. A fragility fracture (fall from standing height) warrants osteoporosis assessment (FRAX / DEXA).
What & why
📷
Image placeholder: DEXA scan report with a T-score graph (osteoporosis ≤ −2.5), and a lateral spine X-ray showing a vertebral wedge/crush fracture
Osteoporosis = a significant reduction in bone density (osteopenia = a less severe decrease) → weak bones prone to fracture.
The core concept: osteoporosis is low bone density (a quantity problem) — but the bone that is there is normally mineralised (unlike osteomalacia's mineralisation defect or osteogenesis imperfecta's collagen defect) — there's just less of it. Hence the bone profile (Ca/phosphate/PTH/ALP) is NORMAL. It's a silent disease → the approach is risk assessment (FRAX/QFracture + DEXA) to treat people before they fracture, centred on bisphosphonates + reversible risk factors.
  • T-score ≤ −2.5 = osteoporosis; −1 to −2.5 = osteopenia; weekly oral bisphosphonate is first-line.

The rule: osteoporosis has a NORMAL bone profile (Ca, PTH, phosphate, ALP all normal) — this distinguishes it from osteomalacia (low Ca/phosphate, high ALP/PTH) and Paget's (isolated very high ALP).

Osteoporosis is SILENT until it fractures — symptoms are secondary to fractures. Classic fragility-fracture sites:

SiteNote

High-yield: a fragility fracture = a fracture from low-energy trauma (a fall from standing height or less) → always prompts osteoporosis assessment. In a young man with a fragility fracture → check testosterone (hypogonadism).
Investigations
  • Bone profile: NORMAL (Ca, PTH, phosphate, ALP) — an abnormal profile points to another diagnosis.
  • DEXA scan — the KEY investigation: measures bone mineral density (mostly femoral neck + lumbar spine), reported as a T-score (SDs above/below a young healthy adult): normal ≥ −1; osteopenia −1 to −2.5; osteoporosis ≤ −2.5; severe/established = ≤ −2.5 + a fragility fracture. (Z-score compares to age-matched peers — used in the young.)
  • Testosterone in a young man with a fragility fracture; screen for secondary causes if atypical (myeloma screen, TFTs, coeliac, vitamin D).
Fracture-risk assessment
  • Assess: anyone on long-term corticosteroids or with a previous fragility fracture; anyone 50+ with risk factors; all women 65+, all men 75+.
  • Calculate 10-year risk with QFracture (or FRAX) → ≥10% → consider DEXA. (FRAX and QFracture aren't interchangeable — NOGG thresholds use FRAX; FRAX can incorporate the DEXA result, QFracture cannot.)
  • DEXA without a calculation in any patient >50 with a fragility fracture. Treat without DEXA in: vertebral fracture, or >65 with a previous fragility fracture.
Management
The principle: reversible risk factors + calcium/vitamin D; bisphosphonates first-line; correct calcium/vitamin D before starting; reassess after 3–5 years.
  • Reversible risk factors: physical activity, healthy weight, stop smoking + alcohol, falls prevention. Calcium + vitamin D if intake inadequate (calcium ≥1000 mg + vitamin D 400–800 IU). Acute vertebral fracture: bed rest 1–2 weeks + strong analgesia.
  • 1st line: bisphosphonates — alendronate 70 mg weekly, risedronate 35 mg weekly, or zoledronic acid 5 mg IV yearly. Mechanism: reduce osteoclast activity (↓recruitment + osteoclast apoptosis) → ↓resorption.
  • Side effects: reflux/oesophageal erosions, atypical (femoral) fractures, osteonecrosis of the jaw (→ dental checks before/after) and external auditory canal. Contraindicated eGFR <35. Take on an empty stomach with a full glass of water, sit upright 30 min before eating. Correct hypocalcaemia/vitamin D deficiency BEFORE starting. Reassess after 5 years (oral) / 3 years (IV) with FRAX + DEXA.

What it is
↓ bone density (osteopenia = milder); silent until FRACTURE; bone profile NORMAL (Ca/phosphate/PTH/ALP) — distinguishes from osteomalacia/Paget's.
Risk factors
Older age, post-menopausal (↓oestrogen), steroids, smoking/alcohol, low BMI, low Ca/vit D, immobility, CKD; drugs (SSRIs, PPIs, anti-epileptics).
Fragility fractures
Vertebrae (crush), hip (neck of femur), distal radius (Colles').

Normal ≥ −1; osteopenia −1 to −2.5; osteoporosis ≤ −2.5; young man with fragility fracture → check testosterone.

QFracture/FRAX (all women 65+, men 75+, 50+ with risk factors, steroids/prior fracture); ≥10% → DEXA.
Management
Lifestyle + Ca/vit D; 1st-line bisphosphonate (alendronate 70mg weekly, ↓osteoclasts); take upright/empty stomach; SEs = oesophagitis, atypical fractures, osteonecrosis of jaw; correct Ca/vit D first; reassess 5y (3y IV).
Alternatives
Denosumab (anti-RANKL, if eGFR <30), teriparatide (anabolic/PTH), romosozumab (anti-sclerostin), HRT/raloxifene.
What & why
📷
Image placeholder: osteomalacia — Looser's zones (pseudofractures) on X-ray; and childhood rickets with bowed legs, widened wrists and a “rickety rosary”
Osteomalacia = defective bone MINERALISATION causing "soft" bones — resulting from insufficient vitamin D.
The core concept: a mineralisation problem — there's enough bone matrix (osteoid), but it isn't hardened with calcium/phosphate → soft, painful bones prone to bending/fracturing (the opposite of osteoporosis, which has less bone of normal quality). The clinical anchor is the biochemistry: low calcium/phosphate + high ALP + high PTH (secondary hyperparathyroidism) — the mirror image of osteoporosis. The cause is almost always vitamin D deficiency → treatment is vitamin D replacement.
  • The same process in CHILDREN (before growth plates fuse) causes RICKETS — soft bones + bone deformity in a growing child.
The decisive fork: osteomalacia vs osteoporosis (biochemistry)

The rule: osteomalacia = LOW Ca/phosphate + HIGH ALP/PTH + LOW vitamin D; osteoporosis = NORMAL bone profile → the biochemistry distinguishes them. Classic osteomalacia feature: bone pain + proximal myopathy, Looser's zones.
Pathophysiology & causes
  • Vitamin D's role: promotes calcium + phosphate absorption (gut) + deposition in bone → without it, bone can't mineralise (osteoid accumulates unmineralised). Its major source is skin photosynthesis after UVB sunlight (also dietary).
  • Secondary hyperparathyroidism: low vitamin D → ↓calcium absorption → low serum calcium → PTH rises to compensate → mobilises calcium from bone (worsening the disease) + raises ALP.

FeatureDetail
Bone pain + tendernessdiffuse, aching bone pain
Proximal myopathymuscle weakness → a waddling gait
Fracturespathological fractures — especially the femoral neck

Looser's zones (pseudofractures) — high-yield: low-density bands running perpendicular to the cortex — the classic X-ray sign. Bone pain + proximal muscle weakness (waddling gait) = osteomalacia. Rickets (children): bowing of the legs (genu varum), "rickety rosary" (costochondral swelling), widened wrists/growth plates, delayed fontanelle closure, frontal bossing.
Investigations
  • Serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D — the key test: <25 nmol/L = deficiency; 25–50 = insufficiency.
  • Biochemistry: low calcium (or normal), low phosphate (or normal), high ALP, high PTH (secondary hyperparathyroidism).
  • Imaging: X-ray — osteopenia + Looser's pseudofractures (low-density bands perpendicular to the cortex); DEXA — low bone mineral density.
The rule: low vitamin D + low Ca/phosphate + high ALP + high PTH + Looser's zones = osteomalacia.
Management
The principle: replace vitamin D (colecalciferol) + calcium; treat the underlying cause.
  • 1st line: colecalciferol (vitamin D3) — loading regimens (e.g. 50,000 IU, typically weekly for several weeks) → maintenance; ensure adequate calcium intake.
  • Treat the cause: malabsorption (coeliac/IBD) → treat + higher-dose/parenteral vitamin D; CKD (renal osteodystrophy) → activated vitamin D (alfacalcidol/calcitriol) (the kidney can't 1α-hydroxylate) + phosphate control; phosphate-wasting → phosphate ± specific therapy.
  • Monitor vitamin D, Ca, phosphate, ALP, PTH; symptoms + myopathy improve. Prevention: sunlight, dietary vitamin D, supplementation in at-risk groups.
Exam pearls
What it is
Defective bone MINERALISATION → soft bones, from vitamin D deficiency; rickets = the same in children (bone deformity).
Biochemistry
LOW calcium + LOW phosphate + HIGH ALP + HIGH PTH (secondary hyperparathyroidism) + LOW vitamin D — the mirror image of osteoporosis (normal profile).
Features
Bone pain + tenderness + PROXIMAL MYOPATHY (waddling gait), fractures (esp. femoral neck); may be asymptomatic.
Looser's zones
Low-density bands perpendicular to the cortex — the classic X-ray sign.
Rickets (children)
Bowed legs, rickety rosary, widened wrists, frontal bossing.
Ix & Mx
Serum 25-OH vitamin D (<25 deficient, 25–50 insufficient) + the biochemistry + Looser's zones; colecalciferol loading (e.g. 50,000 IU) + calcium; treat the cause (activated vitamin D in CKD).
What & why
📷
Image placeholder: Paget's disease — X-ray of a bowed, thickened tibia and skull with “cotton-wool” sclerosis / bony enlargement
Paget's disease of bone = a focal disorder of bone REMODELLING — excessive, uncoordinated bone turnover (resorption + formation) from increased osteoclast AND osteoblast activity.
The core concept: normal remodelling is a balanced, coordinated cycle; in Paget's it becomes overactive AND disorganised → structurally abnormal, enlarged, misshapen bone with patchy sclerosis + lysis. This weak, deformed, hypervascular bone explains everything: bone pain, deformity, fractures, nerve compression (hearing loss), and high-output heart failure. The diagnostic anchor is an isolated raised ALP with normal calcium/phosphate; treatment is bisphosphonates.
  • Classic patient: an older male with bone pain + an isolated rise in ALP; particularly affects the axial skeleton.
The decisive fork: vs the other metabolic bone diseases (biochemistry)

Problemdisordered remodelling↓ quantitydefective mineralisation

Phosphatenormalnormallow
ALPisolated HIGH (often >1000)normalhigh
PTHnormalnormalhigh
The rule: Paget's = ISOLATED raised ALP (often >1000) with NORMAL calcium + phosphate — the classic fingerprint (osteomalacia also raises ALP but with abnormal Ca/phosphate/PTH). Exam trigger: "older man + bone pain + isolated raised ALP" = Paget's until proven otherwise.
Pathophysiology
  • Excessive bone turnover (resorption + formation) from increased osteoclast + osteoblast activity, but NOT coordinated → patchy high density (sclerosis) + low density (lysis).
  • Consequence: enlarged + misshapen bones, structural weakness, pathological fractures (disorganised, structurally weak, hypervascular bone).
  • Three phases: early osteolytic (osteoclast-predominant) → mixed → late sclerotic/osteoblastic — explaining the patchy lytic + sclerotic appearance.
Clinical features

May be asymptomatic (found incidentally — isolated raised ALP or X-ray). Symptomatic:

Bone painthe commonest symptom — deep, aching
Bone deformityenlarged skull, tibial bowing ("sabre tibia")
Fracturespathological fractures (weak bone)
Hearing lossskull involvement compressing CN VIII / ossicles
Bones affected: skull, spine, pelvis, and long bones of the lower limbs (axial skeleton + long bones). Classic presentation: an older patient with bone pain, an enlarging skull (hats no longer fit), bowed tibia, hearing loss, and warmth over the affected bone (hypervascularity).
Investigations
  • Bloods: isolated raised ALP (often >1000 U/L); normal calcium + phosphate; PTH/vitamin D normal.
X-ray findingDetail
Bone enlargement + deformity—
Osteoporosis circumscriptawell-defined osteolytic lesions, less dense than normal bone (lytic phase, esp. skull)
"Cotton wool" skullpoorly-defined patchy areas of increased + decreased density (mixed phase)
V-shaped lytic defects in long bones"blade of grass"/"flame" lytic front advancing along the bone
Radionuclide bone scan assesses the extent/distribution (increased uptake). The rule: isolated raised ALP + normal Ca/phosphate + characteristic X-ray = Paget's.
Management
The principle: bisphosphonates (switch off the overactive osteoclasts) + analgesia; monitor with ALP.
  • Mainstay: bisphosphonates — decrease osteoclast activity → restore normal bone metabolism; oral risedronate or IV zoledronate (a single IV zoledronate infusion is often very effective).
  • Other: calcitonin if bisphosphonates unsuitable; analgesia (NSAIDs) for bone pain; calcium + vitamin D if needed (ensure replete before bisphosphonates).
  • Indications to treat: bone pain, or to prevent complications at high-risk sites (skull, weight-bearing bones, near joints, before orthopaedic surgery); asymptomatic disease may just be monitored.
  • Monitoring: serum ALP + symptoms (ALP falls with successful treatment). Surgery for fractures, deformity, or joint replacement (secondary osteoarthritis).

Hypervascular Pagetic bone → high-output cardiac failure (extensive disease). Also secondary osteoarthritis, spinal stenosis/nerve compression, hypercalcaemia (if immobilised).

Focal disorder of DISORDERED bone remodelling (overactive + uncoordinated osteoclasts + osteoblasts) → enlarged, misshapen, weak, hypervascular bone (patchy sclerosis + lysis).

Bisphosphonates (risedronate/zoledronate) — ↓osteoclast activity; analgesia (NSAIDs); calcitonin if unsuitable; monitor ALP.

Hearing loss, HIGH-OUTPUT heart failure (hypervascularity), OSTEOSARCOMA (poor prognosis — new focal pain/swelling), secondary osteoarthritis.
MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Bone & Joint Infecti:
Overview — bone & joint infection
Infection of a joint (septic arthritis) or bone (osteomyelitis), usually bacterial — S. aureus is commonest — spreading haematogenously, by direct inoculation or from contiguous tissue.
The organising principle: both are limb- and joint-threatening emergencies. Take cultures before antibiotics, image/aspirate promptly, and involve orthopaedics early — many need surgical washout or debridement.
Septic arthritisOsteomyelitis
Presentationhot, swollen, exquisitely painful joint, ↓ROMbone pain, fever, local tenderness

Never attribute a hot joint to gout without aspirating to exclude sepsis. Consider osteomyelitis in the diabetic foot (probe-to-bone) and the child's hip/long bones.
What & why
📷
Clinical image placeholder: acutely hot, swollen, erythematous knee (septic arthritis); and a turbid/purulent synovial-fluid aspirate
Septic arthritis = infection within a joint (bacterial invasion of the synovial space) — a medical/orthopaedic emergency.
The core concept: a "don't miss, don't delay" diagnosis — bacteria destroy articular cartilage within days → irreversible joint destruction, and it can seed sepsis. So: any acutely hot, swollen, painful joint is septic arthritis until proven otherwise → aspirate the joint (before antibiotics) → start empirical IV antibiotics urgently. Commonest organism Staphylococcus aureus; commonest joint the knee.
  • Joints are infected by direct injury or blood-borne (haematogenous) spread; higher risk in the immunosuppressed, pre-existing joint disease, and prosthetic joints.
The decisive fork: septic, or a non-infective arthritis?
Septic arthritisCrystal arthritis (gout/pseudogout)
Onsetacute, hot, very painful, systemically unwell/feveracute, hot, painful (gout — big toe)
Key testsynovial fluid: bacteria/high WCC, culturecrystals (urate/pyrophosphate) on polarised light
Overlapcrystals + infection can coexist — don't assume it's "just gout"
The rule (high-yield): you cannot reliably distinguish septic arthritis from gout/pseudogout clinically → aspirate every acutely hot joint and send for microscopy, culture, AND crystals (crystals present doesn't exclude co-existing infection). Other differentials: reactive arthritis, a flare of rheumatoid arthritis, haemarthrosis.
Microbiology
OrganismNote
Staphylococcus aureusthe commonest overall
Streptococcisecond commonest

The two high-yield organisms: Staph aureus (commonest overall); gonococcus (commonest in young sexually active adults).
Clinical features
FeatureDetail
Hot, swollen, painful jointacute; warm to touch + fluctuant
Restricted movementin ~80% — the joint is held still, movement agonising
Feversystemically unwell
High-yield: commonest joint = the knee; usually monoarticular. Acute monoarthritis + fever + refusal to move the joint = septic arthritis until excluded. Consider prosthetic joint infection in any painful prosthesis (may be indolent); in a limping/febrile child use the Kocher criteria (fever, non-weight-bearing, ↑ESR, ↑WCC) to distinguish from transient synovitis.
Investigations
The rule: aspirate the joint + take blood cultures BEFORE starting antibiotics.
  • Synovial fluid sampling (joint aspiration) — the KEY investigation: must be done BEFORE antibiotics; the fluid is opaque, with up to ~75,000 WCC, mostly neutrophils. Send for Gram stain, microscopy + culture (organism/sensitivities), AND crystals.
  • Blood cultures — haematogenous spread is the commonest route, so often positive; take before antibiotics.
  • Bloods: raised WCC, CRP, ESR.
  • Imaging: X-ray (baseline; often normal early → later joint destruction); ultrasound to guide aspiration (esp. hip).
Management
The principle: urgent joint aspiration/washout + prolonged IV antibiotics — an emergency to save the joint.
  • IV antibiotics (Gram-positive cocci cover): 1st line IV flucloxacillin; penicillin allergy → clindamycin (or vancomycin); add vancomycin if MRSA risk; gonococcal → ceftriaxone; adjust to culture/sensitivities. Duration 4–6 weeks (IV then oral switch).
  • Joint drainage: needle aspiration to decompress (may need repeated aspiration); arthroscopic lavage (washout) for inadequate response, hip involvement, or prosthetic joints.
  • Prosthetic joint infection: combined orthopaedics + microbiology (surgical washout ± revision/removal of the prosthesis + prolonged antibiotics).
  • Supportive: analgesia, rest/immobilise then physiotherapy, treat sepsis, remove/treat the source.

What it is
Joint infection = medical emergency (destroys cartilage within days); any acutely hot, swollen, painful joint = septic until proven otherwise.
Organism/joint
Commonest organism = Staph aureus; commonest joint = knee; usually monoarticular + fever + restricted movement; gonococcus in young sexually active adults (migratory + tenosynovitis + rash).
Route
Haematogenous (commonest) or direct injury.
KEY investigation
Joint aspiration BEFORE antibiotics → opaque fluid, ~75,000 WCC (neutrophils), Gram stain/culture + crystals (crystals don't exclude infection); + blood cultures.
Can't tell from gout
Cannot distinguish clinically from gout/pseudogout → always aspirate.
Management
IV flucloxacillin (clindamycin if penicillin-allergic) for 4–6 weeks + needle aspiration/decompression ± arthroscopic lavage; MRSA → vancomycin; gonococcus → ceftriaxone.
Special contexts
Prosthetic joint → orthopaedics + microbiology (washout ± revision); child with hot joint → Kocher criteria (vs transient synovitis).
What & why
📷
Imaging placeholder: osteomyelitis — X-ray showing periosteal reaction with sequestrum and involucrum, and MRI showing bone-marrow oedema
Osteomyelitis = a bacterial infection of bone and/or bone marrow.
The core concept: the bone equivalent of septic arthritis — if untreated → bone destruction, dead bone (sequestrum), and chronic relapsing infection. Key anchors: commonest organism Staph aureus (with the crucial exception of Salmonella in sickle cell disease), investigation of choice is MRI, treatment is prolonged antibiotics ± surgical debridement. Reaches bone by haematogenous spread (commonest) or direct contamination.
  • Ranges from acute (rapid, treatable) to chronic (dead bone, sinus tracts, relapsing — needs longer treatment + surgery); higher risk with diabetes, IVDU, immunosuppression, prosthetic material.
The decisive fork: route, and acute vs chronic?

(a) Route of infection:

RouteDetail
Haematogenous spreadthe commonest — blood-borne from a distant infection; classically the metaphysis of long bones in children, or the vertebrae in adults
Direct contaminationoperation, fracture site, penetrating trauma, or contiguous spread (e.g. diabetic foot ulcer)
(b) Acute vs chronic: acute = recent onset, treatable with antibiotics (± limited surgery); chronic = established infection with dead bone (sequestrum), new bone (involucrum), sinus tracts, and relapses → needs prolonged antibiotics + surgical debridement; often follows inadequately treated acute infection or prosthetic/implant infection.

OrganismContext

PseudomonasIVDU, puncture wounds through trainers

The two high-yield associations: Staph aureus = commonest overall; Salmonella = commonest in sickle cell ("sickle cell → salmonella").
Risk factors
  • Open fractures, orthopaedic operations, diabetes mellitus, IVDU, immunosuppression, peripheral arterial disease.
  • Also: sickle cell disease (Salmonella), prosthetic joints/implants, chronic wounds/ulcers (diabetic foot), penetrating trauma.
Clinical features
FeatureDetail
Feversystemic infection
Pain + tendernesslocalised to the specific bone infected — it should NOT radiate (unlike discitis)
Erythemaoverlying
Swellinglocal
High-yield: the pain is localised to the infected bone and does NOT radiate — a useful discriminator from discitis (which can radiate). Chronic osteomyelitis → a discharging sinus tract, chronic pain, relapses. Vertebral (spinal) → back pain + fever (consider in IVDU; TB → Pott's disease).
Investigations
  • MRI = gold standard — the most sensitive investigation; detects early bone/marrow changes, soft-tissue involvement, abscesses.
  • Bloods: raised inflammatory markers — WBC, CRP, ESR.
  • Blood cultures — may be positive for the causative organism.
  • Bone cultures / biopsy — to establish the organism + sensitivities; the definitive way to guide targeted therapy.
  • X-ray: often normal early (bone changes take ~1–2 weeks) — later periosteal reaction, lucency, sequestrum/involucrum in chronic disease.
  • In sickle cell, distinguishing osteomyelitis from a bone infarct/vaso-occlusive crisis is a classic difficulty — MRI + cultures help.
Management
The principle: prolonged antibiotics ± surgical debridement — longer for chronic disease; get cultures to target therapy.
  • Acute osteomyelitis: 6 weeks of flucloxacillin, possibly with rifampicin or fusidic acid for the first 2 weeks (better bone/biofilm penetration); penicillin allergy/MRSA → clindamycin or vancomycin.
  • Chronic osteomyelitis: same antibiotics but for 3+ months.
  • Surgery: surgical debridement of infected/dead bone — essential in chronic disease (remove the sequestrum — antibiotics can't penetrate dead bone).
  • Prosthetic osteomyelitis: may need complete revision surgery to replace the prosthesis.
  • Special contexts: Salmonella (sickle cell) → tailor antibiotics; TB spine (Pott's) → anti-TB therapy; treat the source (e.g. diabetic foot). Tailor to culture/sensitivities once available.

Bacterial infection of bone/marrow; haematogenous (commonest) or direct/contiguous spread.

Commonest = Staph aureus; SICKLE CELL → Salmonella ("sickle cell → salmonella"); IVDU/puncture → Pseudomonas; spine → TB (Pott's).

Open fractures, ortho surgery, diabetes, IVDU, immunosuppression, PAD, sickle cell, prosthetic joints.

Antibiotics + surgical debridement; acute = flucloxacillin 6 weeks (± rifampicin/fusidic acid first 2 weeks; clindamycin/vancomycin if penicillin-allergic/MRSA); chronic = same but 3+ months; prosthetic → revision surgery.
MSK / RHEUMATOLOGY__Heritable Connective:
Overview — heritable connective tissue disorders
Inherited defects of structural proteins (fibrillin, collagen) producing multisystem features across the skeleton, skin, joints, eyes and cardiovascular system.
The organising principle: the defective protein predicts the phenotype — fibrillin-1 (Marfan) → tall habitus + aortic root; collagen (EDS) → hypermobility + skin; type I collagen (OI) → brittle bones.
DisorderDefectHallmark
Marfan syndromefibrillin-1 (FBN1, AD)tall, arachnodactyly, lens dislocation (up), aortic root dilatation

Marfan and vascular EDS carry aortic/arterial rupture risk — cardiac surveillance (echo) is essential. Suspect these in a young person with fractures, dislocations or aortic events out of proportion to trauma.
What & why
Marfan syndrome = an autosomal dominant connective-tissue disorder caused by a defect in the FBN1 gene (chromosome 15) → abnormal fibrillin-1 protein.
The core concept: fibrillin-1 is a key structural glycoprotein of the extracellular matrix (it forms the microfibrils that strengthen connective + elastic tissue), so its defect weakens connective tissue throughout the body — a tall, thin patient with long limbs/fingers + lens dislocation + a dilated aorta. The priority is the cardiovascular risk: aortic root dilation → dissection/rupture is the leading cause of death → lifelong echo surveillance + prophylaxis.
  • Recognised clinically (Ghent criteria) + genetically; the "don't miss" is the aorta.
The decisive fork: Marfan vs its mimics
