The high-yield mimic: homocystinuria shares tall/arachnodactyly + lens dislocation, BUT the lens dislocates DOWNWARD (Marfan = UPWARD), plus learning disability + thrombosis, and it's autosomal recessive → check plasma/urine homocysteine. The lens rule: Marfan = UP (superior); homocystinuria = DOWN — "Marfan looks UP to the stars".
Genetics
  • Autosomal dominant (50% risk to offspring; ~25% de novo mutations).
  • FBN1 gene on chromosome 15 → fibrillin-1, a structural protein of connective/elastic tissue → its loss → weak connective tissue + dysregulated TGF-β (transforming growth factor beta) signalling (the latter drives the aortic pathology — the rationale for ARB therapy).

Also: joint hypermobility, positive thumb (Steinberg) sign (thumb projects beyond the clenched fist) and wrist (Walker-Murdoch) sign, long narrow face.

Cardiovascular (the KEY system): dilation of the aortic sinuses (aortic root) → aneurysm, aortic DISSECTION, aortic regurgitation, mitral valve prolapse. Aortic root dilation → dissection/rupture is the leading cause of death → serial echo surveillance.
  • Respiratory: recurrent pneumothoraces (apical blebs).
  • Ocular: UPWARD/superior lens dislocation (ectopia lentis) — the classic sign; blue sclera; myopia (+ retinal detachment/glaucoma risk).
Diagnosis / investigations
  • Clinical diagnosis using the Ghent criteria (aortic root dilation/dissection + ectopia lentis + FBN1 mutation + systemic score + family history).
  • Echocardiogram — assess + monitor the aortic root (dilation, regurgitation, mitral valve prolapse) — the cornerstone of surveillance.
  • Slit-lamp eye exam (ectopia lentis); genetic testing (FBN1); exclude homocystinuria (plasma/urine homocysteine); CT/MR angiography for the aorta if needed.
Management
The principle: protect the aorta — surveillance + beta-blockers/ARBs + prophylactic surgery — and MDT care of the other systems.
  • Cardiovascular (priority): regular echo surveillance of the aortic root; beta-blockers (or ARBs — losartan) to slow aortic root dilation; prophylactic aortic root replacement at a threshold diameter (~5 cm, or smaller with family history of dissection) — before it dissects; avoid intense isometric/contact/competitive sport.
  • Ocular: ophthalmology (lens, refraction, retinal/glaucoma). Skeletal: monitor/treat scoliosis. Respiratory: manage pneumothoraces.
  • Genetic counselling (autosomal dominant, 50%) + family screening (echo + eyes + genetics). Pregnancy: high risk of aortic dissection → pre-pregnancy aortic assessment + close monitoring.

Autosomal dominant connective-tissue disorder; FBN1 gene (chromosome 15) → fibrillin-1 defect.

Aortic ROOT dilation → aneurysm/DISSECTION (leading cause of death), aortic regurgitation, mitral valve prolapse → echo surveillance.

Echo surveillance + beta-blockers/ARBs (losartan) to slow aortic dilation + prophylactic aortic root surgery; avoid intense/contact sport; high dissection risk in pregnancy.
What & why
Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (EDS) = a group of inherited connective-tissue disorders affecting collagen — classically autosomal dominant, affecting type V collagen (classical EDS; type III = vascular EDS) → joint hypermobility + increased skin elasticity.
The core concept: a collagen defect → tissue that is too stretchy + too fragile. Two hallmarks: hypermobile joints (that dislocate) and hyperextensible, fragile skin (that stretches, bruises, heals poorly). The key distinction is which type — the vascular type is life-threatening (arterial/organ rupture) while the hypermobile type is common + comparatively benign. The Beighton score quantifies hypermobility; management is largely supportive with complication surveillance.
  • The key differential is Marfan syndrome — the other hereditary cause of hypermobility.

The principle: no cure → maintain healthy joints, monitor for complications, manage symptoms — via an MDT.

What & why
Osteogenesis imperfecta (OI), or "brittle bone disease" = an inherited (autosomal dominant) disorder of type 1 collagen → fragile bones that fracture easily.
The core concept: type 1 collagen is the main protein scaffold of bone (and of sclera, teeth, ligaments, and the inner ear), so its defect → brittle bones + extra-skeletal signs (blue sclera, dental problems, hearing loss) — all from the same faulty collagen. The key point: the biochemistry paradox — despite fragile bones, calcium/phosphate/PTH/ALP are all NORMAL (a collagen, not mineralisation, problem) → distinguishes it from rickets/osteomalacia. Also a key differential for non-accidental injury.

  • Autosomal dominant (most types; some recessive/de novo).
  • Abnormality in type 1 collagen — from decreased synthesis of pro-alpha-1 and pro-alpha-2 collagen polypeptides → defective/insufficient type 1 collagen → weak bone matrix.
  • The collagen link: type 1 collagen is in bone, sclera, teeth, ligaments, and the ear → explains the fractures + blue sclera + dental problems + hearing loss together.

The KEY point: adjusted calcium, phosphate, PTH, and ALP are ALL usually NORMAL — because OI is a collagen (matrix) defect, not a mineralisation defect → this distinguishes it from rickets/osteomalacia (low Ca/phosphate + high ALP/PTH).

The principle: no cure → minimise fractures, manage them, maximise function, and treat the associated features — via an MDT.

  • Fracture + orthopaedic management: treat fractures; intramedullary rods to strengthen/straighten long bones; correct deformities/scoliosis. Physiotherapy + OT to maximise strength/mobility.
  • Associated features: hearing (audiology; hearing aids/surgery for otosclerosis), dental care (dentinogenesis imperfecta), ophthalmology.
  • Genetic counselling (autosomal dominant, 50%) + support; safeguarding awareness (distinguish from — and don't miss coexisting — non-accidental injury).

Overview — Muscle Types
The body has three types of muscle — skeletal, cardiac, and smooth — each specialised for a different job, though all generate force by the same fundamental actin-myosin mechanism.
The organising principle: the three muscle types differ in control (voluntary vs involuntary), structure (striated vs not), and behaviour — but all contract via sliding filaments triggered by calcium. Understanding the differences explains their distinct clinical behaviours.
Why it matters: frames the rest of the MSK physiology set (the sliding-filament mechanism, excitation-contraction coupling, the NMJ) and explains why cardiac and skeletal muscle behave differently, and the basis of muscle disorders — cross-ref sliding-filament/excitation-contraction coupling (next subtabs), cardiac action potential (cardiac muscle), GI/vascular smooth muscle, the NMJ.

  • Structure: long, multinucleate, striated fibres; the stripes come from the regular arrangement of sarcomeres (the contractile units — cross-ref sliding-filament note)
  • Control: voluntary, via the somatic nervous system → the neuromuscular junction (ACh → nicotinic receptors — cross-ref NMJ)
  • Behaviour: contracts fast + forcefully but fatigues; graded force via recruitment (more motor units) + frequency (summation → tetanus)

Cardiac Muscle — the heart
  • Structure: striated (like skeletal) but with single central nuclei and joined by intercalated discs containing gap junctions → cells are electrically coupled → the heart contracts as a functional syncytium (all cells fire together)
Key distinguishing features (high-yield)
  • Automaticity: the SA node has intrinsic pacemaker activity → the heart beats without nervous input (cross-ref cardiac AP)
  • Long refractory period (the Ca²⁺ plateau) → cannot be tetanised (essential — a fibrillating pump is useless; cross-ref cardiac AP)
  • Doesn't fatigue (relies on aerobic metabolism — packed with mitochondria)
  • Ca²⁺-induced Ca²⁺ release (extracellular Ca²⁺ triggers release from the SR — more dependent on extracellular Ca²⁺ than skeletal — cross-ref excitation-contraction coupling)
The gap junction point: intercalated discs let the electrical signal spread cell-to-cell → coordinated contraction (why the heart works as one unit).
Smooth Muscle — the involuntary one
  • Structure: not striated (no sarcomeres in the regular arrangement — actin/myosin arranged differently), spindle-shaped, single nucleus
  • Control: involuntary (autonomic NS, hormones, local factors, stretch)
Key features
  • Slow, sustained contraction with low energy cost ("latch mechanism" → can maintain tone for long periods without fatiguing — e.g. vascular tone, sphincters)
  • Two types: single-unit (gap junctions → contracts as a sheet, e.g. gut, bladder — can be spontaneously active) vs multi-unit (individually controlled, e.g. iris, large airways)
  • Calcium mechanism differs: uses calmodulin (not troponin) → Ca²⁺-calmodulin activates myosin light-chain kinase → contraction (cross-ref excitation-contraction)
The clinical relevance: smooth muscle in vessels (BP), airways (asthma), gut (motility), bladder, uterus → the target of many drugs (β-agonists relax airways, etc. — cross-ref autonomic NS).
The Common Mechanism — what unites them
  • Despite the differences, all three contract by the same fundamental mechanism: calcium triggers actin and myosin filaments to slide past each other (the sliding-filament mechanism — cross-ref next subtab)
  • The differences are in the details: skeletal + cardiac use troponin (striated), smooth uses calmodulin; skeletal Ca²⁺ comes mostly from the SR, cardiac needs extracellular Ca²⁺ too

Overview — Sliding-Filament Mechanism & Excitation-Contraction Coupling
This note covers how muscle actually contracts — from the electrical signal arriving to the muscle shortening: the excitation-contraction coupling (linking the AP to calcium release) and the sliding-filament mechanism (how calcium produces force).
The organising principle: contraction is a two-part story — excitation-contraction coupling turns the electrical signal into a calcium release, and the sliding-filament mechanism uses that calcium to make actin and myosin slide past each other (the cross-bridge cycle). Calcium is the trigger, ATP is the fuel.
Why it matters: explains rigor mortis, malignant hyperthermia, muscle fatigue, and the basis of how muscle works (the foundation for muscle disorders) — cross-ref muscle types (the three types), the NMJ (the signal source), cardiac AP (cardiac E-C coupling), the neuron/AP.
The Sarcomere — the contractile unit
Skeletal + cardiac muscle are striated because of the regular arrangement of sarcomeres (the repeating contractile units) — the stripes are the sarcomere's structure:
Component What it is
Thick filamentsMyosin (with heads that bind actin — the "motor")
Thin filamentsActin (+ the regulatory proteins troponin + tropomyosin)
Z-linesThe boundaries of each sarcomere (thin filaments anchor here)
The bandsThe overlapping/non-overlapping regions create the striped appearance
The key regulatory proteins (high-yield): tropomyosin blocks the actin-myosin binding site at rest; troponin binds calcium → moves tropomyosin out of the way → allows contraction (this is where calcium acts).
Excitation-Contraction Coupling — signal into calcium (first half)
The steps linking the electrical signal to calcium release:
Step What happens
1. AP arrivesMotor neuron → NMJ → ACh → muscle depolarises (cross-ref NMJ)
2. AP spreads inwardThe AP travels down the T-tubules (invaginations) into the muscle fibre
3. Calcium releaseThe T-tubule AP triggers the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) to release calcium into the cytoplasm
4. Calcium actsCalcium binds troponin → moves tropomyosin → exposes the actin binding sites → contraction begins
The T-tubule/SR point (high-yield): T-tubules carry the AP deep into the fibre so calcium is released everywhere at once (uniform contraction); the SR is the calcium store → calcium release from the SR is the trigger.
The cardiac difference: cardiac muscle also needs extracellular calcium entering (via the plateau) to trigger SR calcium release (calcium-induced calcium release) → which is why cardiac contraction depends on extracellular Ca²⁺ (cross-ref cardiac AP).
The Sliding-Filament Mechanism / Cross-Bridge Cycle — calcium → force (high-yield)
Once calcium exposes the binding sites, myosin heads pull the actin filaments inward → the sarcomere shortens (the filaments slide, they don't shorten themselves). The cross-bridge cycle (needs calcium + ATP):
Step What happens
1. Cross-bridge formationThe myosin head binds the exposed actin site
2. Power strokeThe myosin head pivots → pulls the actin filament inward (the sarcomere shortens) → ADP + Pi released
3. DetachmentATP binds myosin → myosin releases the actin
4. Re-cockingATP is hydrolysed → the myosin head re-cocks, ready for the next cycle
The cycle repeats as long as calcium + ATP are present → repeated cycles progressively shorten the muscle (like a rope being pulled hand-over-hand).
The two essentials (high-yield):
  • Calcium = the trigger (exposes binding sites via troponin)
  • ATP = the fuel (needed for both the power stroke and detachment) → no ATP → myosin can't detach → the muscle stays locked (see rigor mortis below)
Relaxation — turning it off
  • Contraction stops when the signal ends: the AP stops → calcium is pumped back into the SR (by a Ca²⁺ ATPase — using ATP) → calcium falls → troponin releases calcium → tropomyosin re-blocks the binding sites → the cross-bridges stop → the muscle relaxes
The point: relaxation is active (needs ATP to pump calcium back) → which is why ATP depletion prevents relaxation (rigor).

Overview — The Neuromuscular Junction
The neuromuscular junction (NMJ) is the specialised synapse where a motor neuron meets a skeletal muscle fibre — the point where the nervous system's command becomes muscle contraction.
The organising principle: it's a chemical synapse using acetylcholine (ACh) acting on nicotinic receptors — highly reliable (one nerve AP normally always triggers a muscle AP), and rich in clinical targets: its diseases (myasthenia, Lambert-Eaton), toxins (botulinum, organophosphates), and drugs (muscle relaxants) all map onto specific points in the process.
Why it matters: underpins myasthenia gravis, Lambert-Eaton, muscle relaxants in anaesthesia, botulinum toxin, and organophosphate poisoning — cross-ref synaptic transmission (the general synapse principles), sliding-filament (what happens next — the muscle contracts), myasthenia gravis, anaesthesia.
Structure & Transmission Sequence — the spine
The NMJ has a presynaptic terminal (motor nerve ending), a synaptic cleft, and a postsynaptic membrane (the muscle's motor end plate, folded to pack in receptors). Transmission follows the standard synaptic sequence (cross-ref synaptic transmission):
Step What happens
1. AP arrivesAt the motor nerve terminal
2. Calcium influxVoltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels open → Ca²⁺ enters
3. ACh releaseCa²⁺ triggers vesicles to release acetylcholine into the cleft
4. Receptor bindingACh binds nicotinic ACh receptors on the muscle end plate → opens ion channels → depolarisation (the "end-plate potential")
5. Muscle APThe end-plate potential triggers a muscle action potential → contraction (cross-ref sliding-filament)
6. TerminationAcetylcholinesterase breaks down ACh in the cleft → stops the signal
The reliability point: the NMJ has a large "safety margin" — far more ACh is released than needed → so one nerve AP reliably triggers one muscle AP (unlike CNS synapses that need summation). Diseases work by eroding this safety margin.
The two key molecular players: nicotinic ACh receptors (postsynaptic) and acetylcholinesterase (terminates the signal) — both are drug/disease targets.

The myasthenia vs Lambert-Eaton distinction (high-yield): both cause weakness, but myasthenia = postsynaptic (receptor), worsens with use; Lambert-Eaton = presynaptic (Ca²⁺ channel/↓ACh release), improves with use + paraneoplastic.

Overview — Bone Physiology & Remodelling
Bone is a living, dynamic tissue — constantly being broken down and rebuilt (remodelled) throughout life — that provides structural support, protects organs, and acts as the body's calcium reservoir.
The organising principle: bone is in continuous turnover, balanced between osteoblasts (build bone) and osteoclasts (break down bone) — and this balance is controlled by the calcium-regulating hormones (PTH, vitamin D, calcitonin) and mechanical load. Tipping the balance causes the metabolic bone diseases.
Why it matters: underpins osteoporosis, osteomalacia/rickets, Paget's disease, CKD bone disease, and the bone drugs (bisphosphonates) — cross-ref calcium homeostasis (PTH/vitamin D — the controllers), CKD bone disease, osteoporosis, the metabolic bone conditions.
Bone Structure & Composition — form fits function
Bone = a mineralised matrix:
Component Role
Organic (collagen, ~⅓)Provides flexibility/tensile strength (the framework)
Mineral (hydroxyapatite = calcium + phosphate, ~⅔)Provides hardness/compressive strength + the calcium store
Two types: cortical (compact) bone (dense, the shaft — strength) + trabecular (cancellous/spongy) bone (metabolically active, the ends/vertebrae — where turnover + osteoporotic fractures happen).
The dual role: bone is both structural and a calcium reservoir → these can conflict (the body will sacrifice bone to maintain blood calcium — see PTH below).

OsteoclastsBreak down (resorb) bone (release calcium + phosphate)Macrophage/monocyte lineage (haematopoietic)

The memory hook: osteoBlasts Build; osteoClasts Consume (resorb). The osteoclast origin point: osteoclasts come from the monocyte/macrophage lineage (haematopoietic) — relevant to how some drugs work.
Bone Remodelling — the continuous turnover cycle (core)
  • Bone is constantly remodelled (~10% replaced per year) in a coupled cycle:
    • Osteoclasts resorb old/damaged bone → then osteoblasts lay down new bone → mineralised
    • The coupling: resorption and formation are normally balanced → bone mass stays constant
  • Why remodel? repairs microdamage, adapts to mechanical load (Wolff's law — bone remodels along lines of stress → weight-bearing exercise builds bone), and releases/stores calcium for homeostasis
The balance principle (high-yield): osteoblast activity = osteoclast activity → stable bone; tipping it →
  • ↑resorption (osteoclasts win) → bone loss → osteoporosis
  • ↓formation or ↓mineralisation → weak bone → osteomalacia
Hormonal Control — the calcium-regulating hormones

Overview — Calcium in Muscle & Bone
Calcium is central to both MSK tissues — it's the trigger for muscle contraction and the structural mineral (and reservoir) of bone — so this note gathers calcium's roles in the MSK system specifically.
The organising principle: calcium plays three distinct MSK roles — (1) intracellular calcium triggers muscle contraction, (2) extracellular/blood calcium sets neuromuscular excitability, and (3) bone calcium provides structure + acts as the body's reservoir. These are governed by the calcium-regulating hormones (PTH, vitamin D — detailed in the calcium homeostasis note).
Why it matters: explains tetany in hypocalcaemia, muscle contraction, the metabolic bone diseases, and why the skeleton is sacrificed to maintain blood calcium — cross-ref sliding-filament/E-C coupling (the contraction trigger), bone physiology (the reservoir), calcium homeostasis (the endocrine regulation — not repeated here), the NMJ.

The key distinction (high-yield, often confused): intracellular calcium (the contraction trigger, released from the SR) is a separate pool from extracellular/blood calcium (which sets excitability). Blood calcium disorders (hypo/hypercalcaemia) affect excitability, not directly the contraction machinery.
Calcium as the Contraction Trigger — the muscle role
  • Inside the muscle, calcium is the trigger for contraction (full detail in the sliding-filament/E-C coupling note):
    • AP → T-tubules → SR releases calcium → calcium binds troponin → moves tropomyosin → exposes actin binding sites → cross-bridge cycle → contraction
    • Relaxation = calcium pumped back into the SR (active, uses ATP)
The point for this note: this intracellular calcium comes from the SR store (in skeletal muscle) — it's tightly controlled and separate from blood calcium; in cardiac muscle, extracellular calcium also contributes (calcium-induced calcium release — cross-ref cardiac AP). (The mechanism is fully in the sliding-filament note — here the point is just that calcium is the on-switch for contraction.)
Calcium & Neuromuscular Excitability — the MSK-specific bit (high-yield)
Extracellular (blood) calcium sets the excitability of nerve + muscle membranes — and this is where blood calcium disorders show up as MSK/neuromuscular symptoms:
  • Calcium stabilises the membrane: it sits on the membrane and raises the threshold for firing (makes it harder to depolarise)
  • ↓Blood calcium (hypocalcaemia) → membrane less stable → hyperexcitable → tetany (spontaneous nerve/muscle firing): cramps, carpopedal spasm, Trousseau's + Chvostek's signs, perioral tingling, and in severe cases laryngospasm/seizures
  • ↑Blood calcium (hypercalcaemia) → membrane more stable → hypoexcitable → weakness, lethargy, hyporeflexia (the "groans/moans" — muscle weakness)
The counterintuitive point (high-yield): low calcium → MORE excitable (tetany); high calcium → LESS excitable (weakness) — the opposite of what students expect, because calcium stabilises the membrane (it's not directly doing the firing).
The alkalosis link (high-yield): it's the ionised (free) calcium that matters. Alkalosis increases calcium binding to albumin → ↓ionised calcium → tetany (why hyperventilation causes perioral tingling + carpopedal spasm despite normal total calcium).
The albumin correction: total calcium must be corrected for albumin (low albumin → low total but normal ionised).
Calcium in Bone — structural + reservoir role
Bone holds ~99% of the body's calcium as hydroxyapatite (calcium phosphate) — serving two roles that can conflict:
Role Detail
StructuralHydroxyapatite gives bone its hardness/compressive strength
ReservoirBone is the body's calcium bank — calcium is released (resorption) or stored (formation) to maintain blood calcium
The calcium-vs-bone conflict (the key concept): maintaining blood calcium takes priority over the skeleton → when blood calcium falls, PTH resorbs bone to release calcium → so chronically high PTH (hyperparathyroidism, CKD) → bone loss (the body sacrifices bone to defend blood calcium) — cross-ref bone physiology + calcium homeostasis.
(The bone cell mechanism — osteoblasts/osteoclasts, remodelling — is in the bone physiology note; here the point is bone as the calcium reservoir.)
The Regulators — cross-ref, not repeated
  • Blood calcium is kept constant by PTH (↑calcium: resorbs bone, renal reabsorption, activates vitamin D) + vitamin D (↑gut calcium absorption) — the full cascade, the vitamin D activation pathway, and the diagnostic patterns are in the calcium homeostasis note (cross-ref)
The MSK-relevant summary: these hormones keep blood calcium in the tight range needed for normal neuromuscular excitability — and they do it partly by drawing on the bone reservoir (the link between the regulation and the bone diseases).
